Within the Town Planning Authority, a meeting scheduling process involves three groups working together. The process begins in the Coordination Unit, where staff draft a schedule of meetings. Once the draft is complete, they add the draft dates to all calendars.

The Support Officer then takes over by checking the dates that were added to the calendars. After reviewing them, the Support Officer suggests modifications based on their assessment.

The Coordination Unit receives these suggested modifications and rechecks all dates accordingly. They then look for potential conflicts in the schedule. Once conflicts have been identified and addressed, they send the final schedule to Committee Members.

Upon receiving the final schedule, the Committee Members check their diaries for availability. They then advise the Coordination Unit of any conflicts they have identified, at which point the process concludes.

The process begins when the GO (Grid Operator) requests measurements from the MSP (Metering Service Provider). Upon receiving this request, the MSP checks the received request to determine its validity.

Based on this check, one of two paths is taken. If the request is not valid or cannot be fulfilled, the MSP denies the request of the GO, and the process concludes.

If the request is valid, the MSP proceeds to perform the measurement. After completing the measurement, another decision point is reached. If there was a failure during the measurement process, the MSP informs the GO about the failure, after which the process moves toward completion.

If the measurement was successful, the MSP transmits the measured values to the GO. The GO then processes the measured values and subsequently sends the changed values back to the MSP. Following this, the GO transmits the readings to the SP (Service Provider).

Both paths—whether the GO was informed about a failure or the readings were transmitted to the SP—converge, and similarly, the path where the request was denied also joins at this point. The process then concludes.

The process involves two main participants: TELECO (a telecommunications company) and the Customer.

The process begins when a customer perceives service degradation and communicates this to TELECO's Customer Service Department. The Customer Service Department receives the problem parameters list and enters a problem report into the system. They then compare the problem report to the customer's Service Level Agreement (SLA) and determine the necessary counter measures.

The process then moves to the Electronic Service department, which determines the customer's significance level. If the customer has a certain significance level, the process proceeds directly. For other significance levels, a further check is made. If the customer is a premium customer, the process links to an extra problem fix process. Otherwise, a detailed problem report is created and sent to Service Management.

Service Management deals with quality violations and investigates the problem. If it's a service management problem, they perform an analysis and create a trouble report. If not, the problem report is sent to Resource Provisioning.

In Resource Provisioning, they check for potential issues. If a problem is detected, they analyse it and create a trouble report. If no problem is detected, they create a service execution notification. Either way, a status report is sent to Service Management.

Service Management then prepares a final status report and determines which actions are required. If there's no problem, the actual service performance is sent to Customer Service. For minor corrective actions, they undertake those actions. For automatic resource restoration, a request is created and sent to Resource Provisioning, where they receive the restoration request, track all possible errors, undertake corrective actions, create a trouble-shooting report, and send it to Service Management.

Service Management then creates a problem resolution report and sends it to Customer Service. Upon receiving either the actual service performance or the problem resolution report, Customer Service simultaneously creates a report for the customer and reports an SLA violation rebate to Billing & Collections. Billing & Collections adjusts the billing accordingly.

Once both activities complete, the report is sent to the customer. The customer receives this report, concluding the process.

The process begins when the customer perceives service degradation and communicates this issue to TELECO. In the Customer Service Department, the problem parameters list is received, triggering a problem report to be entered into the system. This report is then compared to the customer's Service Level Agreement (SLA), after which necessary counter measures are determined.

The case is then forwarded to Electronic Service, where the customer significance is determined. Based on the significance level, if the customer has certain significance, the process continues directly. Otherwise, for premium customers, the case links to an extra problem fix process before proceeding. For other significance levels, the path eventually converges back to the main flow where a detailed problem report is created and sent to Service Management.

Service Management deals with violations of quality and investigates the problem. If it's determined to be a Service Management problem, analysis is performed and a trouble report is created. If not, the problem report is sent to Resource Provisioning.

In Resource Provisioning, potential issues are checked. If a problem is detected, the problem is analysed, a trouble report is created, and a status report is sent to Service Management. If no problem is detected, a service execution notification is created instead, which also leads to sending a status report.

Service Management then prepares the final status report and determines which actions are required. If no problem exists, actual service performance is sent to Customer Service. For minor corrective actions, these are undertaken and a problem resolution report is created. For automatic resource restoration, a request is created and sent to Resource Provisioning, where the restoration request is received, all possible errors are tracked, corrective actions are undertaken, a trouble-shooting report is created and sent back to Service Management, which then forwards it to Customer Service. The problem resolution report is then sent to Customer Service.

In Customer Service, upon receiving either the problem resolution report or actual service performance, two parallel activities occur: a report for the customer is created, and an SLA violation rebate is reported to Billing & Collections, which adjusts the billing accordingly. The recommendation is then passed to a senior claims officer, who checks the recommendation and marks the claim accordingly. At this point, a decision is made based on the assessment.

However, if the recommendation is not acceptable, the senior claims officer sends the claim back to the claims officer. The claims officer then re-examines the claim and writes a new settlement recommendation. This cycle continues until the senior claims officer approves the recommendation and can proceed with finalizing the claim handling process.

If complete, this branch proceeds to synchronize with the engineering branch.

Once both the engineering department has finished preparing for the assembling and the storehouse has completed handling all parts, these parallel branches converge. The engineering department then assembles the bicycle. After assembly is complete, the sales department ships the bicycle, and the process ends.
